name: Digital Fairness Act (proposed)

literature.citation: European Commission (2026), Impact assessment report accompanying the Digital Fairness Act and the simplification of consumer protection rules, SWD(2026) 1101
literature.title: Impact assessment report: Digital Fairness Act and simplification of consumer protection rules
literature.headline: The Commission's impact assessment for the Digital Fairness Act and the Consumer Rights Directive simplification; the Commission expects the consumer package to save EU consumers up to EUR 13.7 billion a year. The Regulatory Scrutiny Board gave a positive opinion with reservations on 3 July 2026.
literature.verified: proposal explanatory memorandum and press release read; report itself not yet read

literature.citation: European Commission (2024), Fitness check of EU consumer law on digital fairness, SWD(2024) 230
literature.title: Fitness check of EU consumer law on digital fairness
literature.headline: Existing EU consumer law does not adequately address dark patterns, addictive design, unfair personalisation and subscription traps; the basis for the Digital Fairness Act.

literature.citation: Whittle, M. et al. (CSES, EY, Tetra Tech, Asterisk, WIK, LE Europe) (2024), Study to support the Fitness Check of EU consumer law on digital fairness and the report on the application of the Modernisation Directive (EU) 2019/2161, final report, study for the European Commission (DG JUST)
literature.authors: Mark Whittle et al. (CSES, EY, Tetra Tech, Asterisk, WIK, LE Europe)
literature.title: Study to support the fitness check of EU consumer law on digital fairness and the report on the application of the Modernisation Directive
literature.venue: Study for the European Commission (DG JUST)
literature.method: evaluation: 101 interviews, consumer survey (10,000 consumers in 10 member states), enterprise survey (1,000 firms), targeted survey, desk research and cost-benefit analysis
literature.headline: Finds ongoing problems with dark patterns and other digital practices; the general principles of the Unfair Commercial Practices Directive cover several of them, but enforcement is weak and traders and authorities lack clear guidance.
literature.verified: final report part 1 read (title page, methodology, conclusions)

literature.citation: European Parliamentary Research Service (2026), Towards a digital fairness act, EPRS briefing
literature.title: Towards a digital fairness act
literature.headline: Parliament's research service briefing on the planned Digital Fairness Act.

literature.citation: Lee-Makiyama, H. & Lozano, C. (2026), Fairness and Politics of Digital Advertising, ECIPE Occasional Paper 06/2026
literature.title: Fairness and Politics of Digital Advertising
literature.method: legal and economic policy analysis of the planned Digital Fairness Act
literature.headline: Argues the planned act does not respond to a clearly identified legislative gap: existing consumer directives already cover most dark patterns, and the problem lies in enforcement; a default-off rule for personalised advertising would shift targeting to cruder proxies.

literature.title: Enabling Innovation and Protecting Consumers in the Agentic Economy: Why the Digital Fairness Act Should Regulate Agentic AI
literature.venue: in AI-Contracting: Münster Colloquia on EU Law and the Digital Economy IX (Nomos), 151-168
literature.outcomes: consumer protection and innovation in agent-based commerce
literature.headline: Argues that AI agents that browse and transact for consumers are a blind spot in the debate on the Digital Fairness Act, and that the act should regulate agentic commerce to enable agent-based business models and protect consumer autonomy, or risk being outdated on entry into force.
literature.summary_plain: A law professor argues the Digital Fairness Act should cover AI agents that shop on consumers' behalf.
literature.citation: Busch, C. (2026), Enabling Innovation and Protecting Consumers in the Agentic Economy: Why the Digital Fairness Act Should Regulate Agentic AI, in AI-Contracting: Münster Colloquia on EU Law and the Digital Economy IX (Nomos), 151-168

literature.authors: Busch, C., Fletcher, A. & Ledger, M. (CERRE)
literature.title: Towards an EU Consumer Law Fit for the Digital Age
literature.outcomes: design of the Digital Fairness Act
literature.headline: Proposes a risk-, design- and ecosystem-based framework that targets genuine gaps and fits with the DSA, with 'fairness by design' as an interpretive principle rather than new duties. Recommends easier subscription cancellation, rules on harmful addictive design, stronger protection of minors, a simple opt-out from personalised advertising and a ban on exploiting situational vulnerabilities.
literature.summary_plain: A Brussels think tank sets out a targeted, proportionate design for the Digital Fairness Act.
literature.citation: Busch, C., Fletcher, A. & Ledger, M. (CERRE) (2026), Towards an EU Consumer Law Fit for the Digital Age, CERRE report, February 2026

literature.title: Towards the Digital Fairness Act
literature.method: policy position; figures from Eurostat and the Commission's fitness check
literature.headline: Fourteen recommendations, including fairness by design and by default, a general ban on dark patterns, addictive design off by default, bans on paid loot boxes, personalisation of offers off by default, restrictions on personalised pricing, considering a ban on personalised advertising, a cancellation button and a ban on reselling event tickets above face value. Cites at least EUR 7.9bn a year of consumer harm from unfair practices (Commission fitness check).
literature.summary_plain: Europe's main consumer group sets out what it wants in the Digital Fairness Act, from banning dark patterns to a one-click cancellation button.
literature.interested_party: Consumer organisation campaigning for stronger rules; co-funded by the EU
literature.citation: BEUC (European Consumer Organisation) (2025), Towards the Digital Fairness Act, BEUC position paper BEUC-X-2025-110, 2 December 2025

literature.title: Digital Fairness in the Age of Agentic Commerce: Analyzing Articles 26 and 27 of the Proposed Digital Fairness Act
literature.outcomes: contractual authority of AI agents, platform access, open agentic commerce
literature.headline: Early analysis of Articles 26 and 27 of the proposed Digital Fairness Act on agentic commerce: when an AI agent's actions bind the consumer, access for agents to platforms, and how to keep agentic commerce open.
literature.summary_plain: A legal scholar reviews the proposal's new rules for AI agents that buy on consumers' behalf.
